scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that backs rewarding good teaching while arguing pay by student results is unfair; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Everyone wants schools to reward the teachers who help their students learn the most.
Some people recommend that teachers' salaries should be based on the academic performance of their students.
I agree that strong teaching deserves reward, but I believe tying pay mainly to student results would be unfair and harmful.
First, the recommendation grows from a fair wish to reward effective teaching.
Connecting some reward to results might encourage teachers to plan their lessons with extra care.
For example, recognising a school's most successful teachers could inspire their colleagues to improve.
This shows that valuing good teaching is a reasonable and worthy goal.
Teachers who work hard and lift their students certainly deserve to be appreciated.
A fair reward for excellent work could also help schools keep their very best staff.
To this extent, the recommendation rests on a sensible intention.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it would be unfair

sentences.text: Second, however, basing pay mainly on student results would be deeply unfair.
How well students perform depends on their home, health, and background, not only on their teacher.
Consider a devoted teacher in a poor area whose students still score lower than those in a wealthy school.
Judging her by results alone would punish her for problems she did not create.
Such a system might also push teachers to teach only to the test and ignore weaker pupils.
Some teachers could even avoid the struggling students who need their help the most.
Pay tied mainly to scores, then, would harm both fairness and learning.
In conclusion, rewarding excellent teaching is a fair and worthy aim.
But linking salaries mainly to student results would ignore all the other forces that shape them.
The wiser approach judges teachers by the quality of their work, not only by their students' scores.
